Forecasts past the data assume that #> the trend's slope does not change (the reference, section 10.4), so their #> intervals leave out any change in it (limn's own reasoning). Reference: Hyndman #> and Athanasopoulos (2021), Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition, #> section 10.4, with 9.5 ('Understanding ARIMA models') and 9.8 ('Prediction #> intervals'). A correlation over time can take the trend's place, and each #> choice is an assumption about the series past the data. If it should return to #> a level: take the trend out, and keep the model's ar1 term. Its forecasts go #> back to zero, so the forecast goes back to the fixed part, and the spread it #> adds levels off (the reference, section 9.5, 'Understanding ARIMA models', and #> section 9.8, 'Prediction intervals', for a series; for a latent term, and for #> ilm_car1(), limn's own reasoning). A trend left in the fixed part still carries #> the forecast, and its uncertainty still grows. If the level should be free to #> move: a random walk, ar = ilm_rw1(~ week | region) (in place of the model's ar1 #> term: a model has one correlation over time), whose intervals keep widening; at #> longer horizons it is the safer choice (the reference, section 10.4). fit <- illume::ilm_model(demand ~ temp + week + (1 | region), data = demand,                          family = "gaussian", ar = illume::ilm_rw1(~ week | region),                          verbose = FALSE) fc_scenario <- ilm_forecast(fit, scenario, nsim = 500) width_r1 <- function(fc) {   a <- as.data.frame(fc)   a <- a[a$region == "R1", ]   setNames(round(a$upper_0.9 - a$lower_0.9, 1), paste0("h", a$horizon)) } rbind(ar1 = width_r1(fc_ar1), rw1 = width_r1(fc_scenario)) #>       h1   h2   h3   h4   h5   h6   h7   h8 #> ar1 10.0 11.4 11.7 12.5 12.5 12.6 12.4 12.5 #> rw1 10.4 11.8 12.8 13.9 14.9 15.6 16.5 17.5
